# A Lightweight Real-Time Object Detection Model for Multimodal Urban Mobility Monitoring on Edge Devices

Tiago Tamagusko1,2\*, Lasith Niroshan1, Titouan Desnoyer1,  Sonia Soubam1, Brian Rogers1, Aura Istrate1, and Francesco Pilla1

1 School of Architecture, Planning and Environmental Policy, University College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland

2 Military Institute of Engineering, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil

| Urban mobility has become increasingly multimodal and dynamic, driven by the rise of remote work and evolving travel behaviors. Traditional survey methods can no longer capture real-time, continuously changing mobility patterns. Computer vision provides a scalable solution; however, most existing models focus on a limited set of road users and are not optimized for deployment on low-power edge devices. A gap remains in detecting emerging and underrepresented modes such as e-scooters in real-world urban environments. Here we present a lightweight object detection model designed to identify nine distinct road user classes: pedestrian, cyclist, e-scooter, car, SUV, motorcycle, bus, delivery van, and truck. We constructed a custom dataset through manual annotation and DINOv3 techniques and compared YOLO architectures (YOLOv5n, YOLOv8n, YOLOv10n, YOLO11n, YOLO12n) for this task. Our optimized YOLO11n model achieved \[mAP@0.5\] with \[model size\] MB and runs at \[FPS\] fps on a Raspberry Pi 5 8GB. Performance validation across controlled video and real-world urban environments demonstrated \[performance drop\]% accuracy reduction in practical deployment conditions. The results demonstrate the potential for efficient model architectures to enable scalable urban mobility monitoring across diverse urban environments. This opens new pathways for data-driven, real-time urban mobility planning and policymaking. |

**Keywords**: *Object Detection, YOLO, Edge Computing, Urban Mobility, Deep Learning, Real-Time Traffic Monitoring*

2. # Data and Methods (\~800 words)

## 2.1 Dataset and Model Development

We constructed a dataset to address gaps in urban mobility detection, with emphasis on emerging transportation modes. YOLO implementations tested already detect Person (renamed pedestrian), Car, Motorcycle, Bus, and Truck. Our goal was to train a model that also detects Cyclists (datasets typically include person and bicycle but not a dedicated cyclist label), E-scooters (people using e-scooters), SUVs, and Delivery Vans. Therefore, our team added four classes that are not present in the COCO dataset, and therefore not in YOLO. Thus, our model is fine-tuned to detect more objects in urban environments, contributing to a better understanding of urban mobility.

We first built the cyclist subset using the ImageNet database. We selected images containing both people and bicycles with an IOU of 0.3, meaning the person and bicycle bounding boxes overlap by 30%. This search returned \[VALUE\] images. Some false positives occurred, such as people walking in front of stationary bicycles. We manually cleaned the results, yielding \[VALUE\] cyclist images after filtering.

In a second step, we applied semi-automated labeling with DINOv3 (Distillation with No Labels version 3), a state-of-the-art self-supervised vision transformer. We then scanned the cyclist dataset to identify occurrences of e-scooters, SUVs, and delivery vans. To increase coverage of these classes, we also collected additional images from the internet using \[METHOD\].

The annotation process combined DINOv3-assisted proposals with manual verification. DINOv3 provided initial object localization through robust feature extraction, which accelerated the workflow. Annotators reviewed and refined the automated suggestions to ensure consistency. Each object instance received a precise bounding box and one of nine labels: pedestrian, cyclist, e-scooter, car, SUV, motorcycle, bus, delivery van, or truck.

Quality control included inter-annotator agreement analysis, which achieved \[agreement score\]% consistency across multiple reviewers. We also conducted a systematic review of \[percentage\]% of annotations and corrected discrepancies where needed. The final dataset contains \[total images\] images with \[total annotations\] annotated objects across all classes.

4. # Conclusions (280 words)

This research successfully developed a comprehensive 9-class urban mobility detection model capable of identifying diverse road users, including pedestrians, cyclists, e-scooters, and various vehicle types. Through systematic comparison of YOLO architectures (YOLOv5n, YOLOv8n, YOLOv10n, YOLO11n, YOLO12n), we demonstrated that \[optimal model\] achieves an optimal balance between model efficiency and detection performance, with \[mAP@0.5\] accuracy while maintaining \[model size\] MB footprint and \[FPS\] inference speed. The dataset construction process revealed significant class imbalances, particularly in underrepresented categories such as e-scooters (\[sample count\] samples) compared to more common vehicle types (\[sample count\] samples). These imbalances likely contributed to varying per-class performance, with challenging detection rates for minority classes (\[e-scooter mAP\] for e-scooters vs. \[car mAP\] for cars), highlighting the ongoing need for targeted data collection strategies.  
The developed model framework demonstrates significant potential for comprehensive real-time mobility data collection across urban environments. By enabling automated detection of emerging transportation modes alongside traditional vehicles, this approach supports data-driven urban planning and policy decisions that can adapt to evolving mobility patterns. The lightweight architecture facilitates scalability for city-wide deployment applications, offering municipal cost-effective alternatives to expensive infrastructure-based monitoring systems. Real-time analytics capabilities enable dynamic traffic management and evidence-based policy interventions.  
Key limitations include model generalization challenges across different urban environments, as performance may vary with distinct architectural styles, traffic patterns, and environmental conditions. Integration challenges with existing traffic management systems require further investigation to ensure seamless deployment in operational contexts. Future work should focus on model adaptation techniques and continuous learning approaches that can accommodate regional variations and evolving mobility trends. Additionally, addressing dataset imbalances through advanced sampling strategies and synthetic data generation could improve minority class detection performance, particularly for emerging mobility modes.

# TASKS:

1\. Data Collection   
• Identify 10 diverse urban mobility videos (8 for training, 2 for testing) covering e-scooters, cyclists, pedestrians, and cars. Images of no intersections, with good density of pedestrians, cyclists and so on.   
• Target at least 500 frames with e-scooters. Aim for 200 delivery vans and 200 SUVs.

2\. Image Extraction Pipeline   
• Build reproducible script to sample frames at fixed interval (e.g., 1 frame every 5 seconds, adjustable).   
• Ensure balanced extraction across videos (avoid heavy dominance by one video).   
• Store metadata: video ID, timestamp, environment type.

3\. Self-Labeling Pipeline (Tiago)   
• Implement semi-automatic labeling workflow using DINOv3, Grounding DINO, and CLIP.   
• Generate bounding box; tag with class probabilities.   
• Export annotations in YOLO format; log accepted/rejected proposals.

4\. Label Verification (Titouan and Sonia)   
• Review and correct auto-labels for consistency with nine-class scheme.   
• Apply guideline document (defines box quality, occlusion rules, etc.).   
• Use consensus checking for 10% of images to measure agreement.

5\. Dataset verification (Titouan and Sonia)   
• Freeze train/val/test split (e.g., 70/30 or 80/20).

6\. Model Training (Tiago)   
• Train YOLO11n with fine-tuning on the curated dataset.   
• Log hyperparameters (epochs, batch size, learning rate, augmentation).   
• Save best model checkpoint, training curves, and evaluation metrics (mAP\\@0.5, per-class AP, FPS baseline).

7\. Paper Writing   
• Introduction: problem context, contributions, gap in edge multimodal detection.   
• Data and Methods: describe video sources, extraction logic, auto-labeling, verification, splits, YOLO11n fine-tuning.   
• Results: report dataset stats, Table 1 (model metrics), Table 2 (per-class AP), Figure 1 (pipeline), Figure 2 (detections), Figure 3 (accuracy–efficiency).   
• Conclusions: highlight YOLO11n performance, deployment readiness, limitations (SUV/delivery van underrepresentation).

8\. Paper Review   
• Co-authors review for clarity, completeness, and technical correctness.   
• Ensure word count ≤3,000 and figures ≤3.   
• Final editing pass before submission.
